content: The term pareidolia, first referenced in 1994 by Steven Goldstein, describes a psychological phenomenon where vague and random stimuli, such as images or sounds, are perceived as meaningful. Common examples include seeing faces or animals in clouds, interpreting the man in the moon, or hearing hidden messages in reversed audio recordings. The word originates from the Greek para(beside, with, or alongside) and eidolon (image, a diminutive of eidos, meaning image, form, or shape). Pareidolia is considered a subset of a broader phenomenon known as apophenia. Religious Examples There have been numerous instances where individuals perceive religious imagery or themes, particularly faces of religious figures, in ordinary objects or phenomena. For example, in 1978, a woman in New Mexico discovered that burn marks on a tortilla she had made resembled the face of Jesus Christ. This tortilla attracted thousands of visitors who came to view the framed object. The rise of online auction platforms like eBay, combined with the publicity surrounding such sightings, has created a market for these items. A notable case involved a grilled cheese sandwich that appeared to depict the Virgin Mary’s face. In another instance, in September 2007, a phenomenon in Singapore known as the monkey tree phenomenon caused a minor social frenzy. A callus on a tree was perceived to resemble a monkey, leading believers to gather and pay homage to what they considered the Monkey God. Rorschach Test The Rorschach inkblot test leverages pareidolia to gain insights into an individual’s mental state. This test is classified as a projective test because it intentionally prompts individuals to project their internal thoughts and feelings onto ambiguous inkblot images. In this context, the projection is a form of directed pareidolia, as the inkblot cards are not designed to resemble any specific object or image. Auditory Pareidolia In 1971, Konstantin Raudive published a book titled Breakthrough, in which he detailed what he believed to be the discovery of electronic voice phenomenon (EVP). EVP is often described as a form of auditory pareidolia, where individuals perceive meaningful sounds or voices in random auditory patterns. Similarly, allegations of backmasking in popular music—where hidden messages are supposedly embedded in reversed audio—are also considered examples of pareidolia. Explanations Carl Sagan Carl Sagan proposed that humans are hard-wired from birth to recognize human faces as a survival mechanism. This innate ability allows people to identify faces even with minimal visual information, such as from a distance or in poor lighting conditions. However, this same mechanism can lead to the misinterpretation of random patterns of light and shadow as faces. Clarence Irving Lewis In his 1929 book Mind and the World Order, epistemologist and logician Clarence Irving Lewis explored the question of how to determine whether a perception is a mirage. As a founder of the philosophical school of conceptual pragmatism, Lewis argued that there is no absolute way to determine whether perceptions are true. Instead, one can only assess whether regarding a perception as true serves a practical purpose. According to this view, two individuals with different purposes may have differing opinions on whether a perception should be considered true. Gallery An example of pareidolia can be seen in an alarm clock that appears to have a sad face. This is a common instance of attributing human-like features to inanimate objects.
